scenes.name: The Electrifying Mojo
scenes.book: Techno Rebels: The Renegades of Electronic Funk
scenes.author: Dan Sicko
scenes.desc: Charles Johnson, criado en Arkansas entre blues, gospel y rock, debutó en la radio en Filipinas y se convirtió en «the Electrifying Mojo» en WAAM, una emisora de rock de Ann Arbor, tras encerrarse a ayunar dos semanas en 1972 para purgarse de todo lo aprendido. Rescató del cuarto de producción lo que se usaba de relleno para anuncios (Tangerine Dream, Kraftwerk: «es evidente que son de mi mismo planeta») y lo mezcló con new wave, funk, rock y soul por «estados de ánimo» y no por formatos, para unir jóvenes y viejos, ricos y pobres, blancos y negros. Nunca se dejó fotografiar; cada noche «aterrizaba» en su nave nodriza y terminaba con su consejo: si llegas al final de la cuerda, hazle un nudo y sigue colgado. Hizo de Parliament, Gap Band y Cameo algo blanco, dio público negro a los B-52’s y la J. Geils Band y le dio a Prince en Detroit uno de sus feudos más fieles. Recelaba del hip hop y del gangsta rap, «la banda sonora insidiosa del genocidio».

podcast.title: Described as Funk's "Id"
podcast.body: Parliament Funkadelic was seen as the "id" of funk, in contrast to Earth Wind & Fire's "super-ego." *The Rolling Stone Encyclopedia of Rock and Roll* characterized them as EWF's "ideological rivals," noting their "down and dirty, but equally eclectic" style. "If Earth, Wind, and Fire represented funk's heightened super-eagong, you might say Parliament Funkadelic was the id."

podcast.title: Extravagant Live Shows
podcast.body: P-Funk's stage shows were noted for being even more extravagant than Earth Wind & Fire's, attracting concertgoers across the spectrum who might not otherwise attend a funk show. "If possible, the P funk's stage show was even more extravagant than Earth Wind and Fire's, and it attracted concert goers across the spectrum who might otherwise not have gone to a funk show."

podcast.title: Focus on Deep Funk over Pop Crossover
podcast.body: George Clinton's dual bands, Parliament and Funkadelic, never achieved the major pop crossover success of Earth Wind & Fire, as neither group landed a Top 10 hit on the Hot 100. However, away from the pop spotlight, Clinton led an elaborate and "crazy funk revolution" with equally spacey LP covers, making P-Funk the prototype for deep 70s funk fans. "Neither Parliament nor Funkadelic ever landed a top 10 hit on the hot 100."

podcast.title: Innovator of 1960s Funk
podcast.body: Parliament Funkadelic is recognized as a key innovator of funk in the 1960s, whose contributions were taken up by a rising generation of syncopated bands and soulful singers in the first half of the 1970s. "the 60s innovations of... Parliament Funkadelic were taken up by a rising generation of syncopated bands and soulful singers."

podcast.title: Most Influential 70s Funk Act
podcast.body: Parliament Funkadelic, led by George Clinton, is considered one of the most influential 70s funk acts, perhaps more so than Earth Wind & Fire, especially concerning their impact on hip hop and later 80s funk. "Maybe among the 70s class of funk acts, Earth Wind and Fire were not as influential as George Clinton and the P funk All Stars."
